screens.title: LVM Snapshots — Copy-on-Write Explained
screens.narratorSegment: A logical volume snapshot is a copy-on-write view of an original logical volume that preserves the state at the time of snapshot creation. The technical mechanism is straightforward: when a snapshot exists, writes to the original volume are redirected so the snapshot keeps the pre-change blocks; the snapshot volume holds the original data until the copy-on-write happens. This allows you to take consistent backups without taking the application offline. A concrete example: create a snapshot with lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name myvol_snap /dev/vg_data/myvol. That snapshot will need enough space to store all changed blocks while it exists. A common misconception is to assume snapshots are full clones; they are not. They only consume additional space for blocks that change. Performance implications matter: the CoW mechanism adds input and output overhead on write paths, so snapshots on busy databases can cause latency. Key operational checks: monitor the snapshot usage with lvs or lvdisplay and plan snapshot lifetimes; ensure snapshot size covers expected write volume; and know that merging a snapshot is destructive to the current LV state, reverting it to the snapshot point in time. In short, snapshots are lightweight and powerful for backups and testing, but they require sizing, monitoring, and an understanding of their performance trade-offs. When would you choose a snapshot vs a full copy? Snapshots for short-lived backups and quick rollbacks; full copies for longer-term archival.

keyIdea.title: LVM Snapshot Core
keyIdea.text: Snapshots are lightweight CoW volumes that represent a volume state at creation time and require monitoring of the snapshot's allocated CoW area.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › LVM Snapshots
Copy-on-Write snapshot — definition
A snapshot stores original blocks as they are changed so you can present a point-in-time view.
Key behavior: after snapshot creation, the original LV continues to accept writes. When a block is overwritten, the previous block is copied into the snapshot area before the write proceeds. That is the copy-on-write action. The snapshot consumes space only for changed blocks, not for the entire volume. Because of that, snapshots are efficient for short-term backups and test rollbacks but can be risky if you underestimate change volume.
Concrete example
Create a 1G snapshot of /dev/vg_data/myvol with lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name myvol_snap /dev/vg_data/myvol.
Common misconception
A snapshot is not a full copy. It only records changed blocks. Treat it as volatile and monitor size.
Key Takeaway

Use snapshots for short-term backups and testing, size the CoW area for expected changed data, and monitor I/O impact.

Operational checks
  • Check snapshot size and usage with lvs or lvdisplay frequently.
  • Avoid long-lived snapshots on high-write workloads to prevent CoW exhaustion.
  • Plan merge operations carefully — merging reverts the LV to the snapshot point.
Check your understanding
Why does a snapshot introduce write latency? Because each overwritten block must be copied to the snapshot area first, adding extra I/O to writes.

screens.title: Create and Restore an LVM Snapshot
screens.narratorSegment: Here's a practical process you will use often: create a snapshot, modify the original data, and merge the snapshot to restore. First, ensure the logical volume is healthy and mounted where required. Create the snapshot with a size that accommodates expected writes: sudo lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name lv_critical_snap /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical. Confirm the snapshot with lvs and ensure the snapshot shows used and available space. Next, while the snapshot exists, you may modify files on the original LV to simulate a failed operation. After changes, if you need to revert, unmount the original filesystem: sudo umount /mnt/appdata. Then, merge the snapshot to revert the LV: sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical_snap. This operation will apply the snapshot image back to the origin — it is destructive to newer changes. After merge completes, remount and verify. A concrete example: if a database write corrupts a table immediately after the snapshot, merging returns the data to the safe pre-change state. Misconception check: do not assume lvconvert --merge preserves new changes. It does not. Always have backups of critical data where possible and test snapshot merges in a controlled environment before using them in production.

keyIdea.title: Snapshot Workflow
keyIdea.text: Create snapshots for quick rollback, unmount before merging, and remember that merging overwrites the current LV state with the snapshot image.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Snapshot Workflow
Steps to create and restore
Follow these numbered steps carefully and verify each status output.
  1. Create snapshot: sudo lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name lv_critical_snap /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical
  2. Verify with lvs: sudo lvs --options lv_name,lv_size,lv_attr,lv_mount
  3. Modify data: simulate changes in /mnt/appdata
  4. Unmount before merge: sudo umount /mnt/appdata
  5. Merge to restore: sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical_snap
  6. Remount and verify: sudo mount /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical /mnt/appdata
Pro Tip

Use small, short-lived snapshots for application-level checkpoints and keep an eye on snapshot usage to avoid overflow.

Example scenario
# Create snapshot
sudo lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name lv_critical_snap /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical

# Simulate change
sudo sh -c 'echo "Modified data after snapshot" >> /mnt/appdata/data.txt'

# Restore by merging
sudo umount /mnt/appdata
sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical_snap
# Remount and verify
sudo mount /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical /mnt/appdata
cat /mnt/appdata/data.txt
Check your understanding
If the snapshot space fills, writes will fail. How would you prevent this? Answer: choose adequate snapshot size and keep snapshot lifetime short.

screens.title: VDO — Deduplication and Compression
screens.narratorSegment: VDO, the Virtual Data Optimizer, offers block-level deduplication and compression to reduce the physical storage required for logically large datasets. Think of it as a layer that presents a large logical device while storing fewer physical blocks by eliminating duplicate data and compressing unique blocks. A practical use case is a VM image store where many images share identical blocks; VDO can dramatically reduce physical usage. To create a VDO volume you run commands like sudo vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=10T and then make a filesystem on the mapped device. A common misconception is that df -h will show VDO savings; df reports the filesystem and device sizes the kernel exposes and won't show dedupe savings. Instead, use vdostats or vdostats --human-readable to measure 'Data Saved' and 'Savings %'. Troubleshooting VDO focuses on device health, ensuring the vdo service is running, and checking vdostats for abnormal activity. Also plan for C P U/memory overhead — deduplication and compression consume resources, so monitor system utilization. In short, VDO is powerful for repeatable block patterns, but validate savings with vdostats and confirm the underlying device is suitable for production workloads.

keyIdea.title: VDO Essence
keyIdea.text: VDO presents a large logical device, while deduplicating and compressing blocks on the underlying storage; verify benefits with vdostats, not df.

content.html:
VDO › Chapter 1.3 › VDO Concepts
What VDO does
Block-level deduplication and compression for physical storage savings.
VDO creates a logical device larger than the physical backing store by hiding duplicate blocks and compressing unique data. This is ideal for workloads with repeated patterns such as VM images or container overlays. But it behaves like a block layer, so when you create a filesystem, the filesystem sees the VDO device as a regular block device. Because of this abstraction, tools that look at filesystem space will not reflect VDO savings; use vdostats to measure actual savings.
Create example
sudo vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=10T
Verify
sudo vdostats --human-readable
When to use VDO
  • VM image stores or containers with many identical blocks.
  • Large datasets with redundant data patterns.
  • Not ideal when underlying device health or CPU/memory are constrained.
Key Takeaway

Use VDO to reduce physical storage when data patterns are redundant. Always verify savings with vdostats and monitor resource overhead.

screens.title: VDO Management & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Managing VDO requires the right sequence: create the VDO device, format it, mount it, and monitor its statistics. After creating a VDO with vdo create, you typically run mkfs on the mapped device, for example sudo mkfs. xfs -K /dev/mapper/myvdo, and mount it to a path. Verification commands include vdostats to track logical and physical usage and vdo status or systemctl status vdo for service health. Troubleshooting often begins by confirming the vdo service is running and the underlying block device is healthy. If vdostats shows no savings, verify the data pattern is deduplicable and check for filesystem options that defeat compression. Another common issue is that df -h will show the device's physical size or logical size as presented; rely on vdostats to measure savings. For performance problems, check C P U and memory consumption since dedupe/compression require cycles. If the VDO device fails to start, inspect kernel messages and syslog for errors related to the device mapper. A concrete diagnostic command sequence is sudo vdo status; sudo vdostats --human-readable; sudo dmesg | tail to find kernel hints. Misconception: stopping a VDO device without unmounting can corrupt the filesystem mapped to /dev/mapper; always unmount before stopping VDO.

content.html:
VDO › Chapter 1.3 › VDO Operations
Management steps
Create, format, mount, and monitor the VDO volume using vdo and vdostats.
  1. Create: sudo vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=10T
  2. Format: sudo mkfs.xfs -K /dev/mapper/myvdo
  3. Mount: sudo mount /dev/mapper/myvdo /mnt/vdo_storage
  4. Verify: sudo vdostats --human-readable
Diagnostics
If issues arise, run vdo status, vdostats, and check dmesg for kernel messages. Confirm the vdo service and device mapper mappings are present.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Is vdo service running and mapped? systemctl status vdo, vdo status
  • Is the underlying device healthy? Check smartctl or dmesg
  • Are CPU/memory adequate for dedupe/compression?
  • Are you using vdostats to measure savings rather than df?
Common Mistake

Stopping VDO without unmounting the mapped filesystem can corrupt the filesystem. Always unmount first.

screens.title: Stratis — Simplified Local Storage
screens.narratorSegment: Stratis provides a higher-level interface for local storage management by creating pools of block devices and exposing filesystems within those pools. Under the covers it leverages existing primitives like LVM and XFS, but the administrator interacts with a simpler stratis CLI and a user-space daemon, stratisd. To create a pool you run sudo stratis pool create mypool /dev/sdd and then create a filesystem with sudo stratis filesystem create mypool myfs. Stratis aims to reduce administrative complexity for developer workflows, thin provisioning, and snapshots without needing manual LVM manipulation. A concrete example: when developers need ephemeral workspaces, Stratis pools let you provision filesystems quickly. Troubleshooting Stratis focuses on the stratisd service, stratis pool list, and stratis filesystem list to confirm configuration. A common misconception is that Stratis replaces all low-level tools — it orchestrates them and stores metadata in a managed layer. Because of that, understanding how Stratis maps to LVM and XFS is valuable when debugging underlying device issues. If a Stratis filesystem fails to mount, check stratisd logs and ensure the underlying block devices are present and healthy. How would you decide between Stratis and manual LVM? Use Stratis for quick, repeatable local pool management; use LVM directly when you need fine-grained control.

keyIdea.text: Stratis simplifies local pool and filesystem management by orchestrating LVM and XFS, exposing an easier CLI and a managed daemon.

content.html:
Stratis › Chapter 1.3 › Stratis Architecture
How Stratis maps to components
Stratis provides a pool abstraction and manages underlying LVM and XFS operations via stratisd.
  • Pool creation: stratis pool create mypool /dev/sdd
  • Filesystem creation: stratis filesystem create mypool myfs
  • Stratis manages thin provisioning, snapshots, and encryption via its layers.
Operational note
If stratisd fails, use journalctl -u stratisd and stratis pool list to inspect state. Verify the underlying devices with lsblk.
When to pick Stratis
Choose Stratis when you want a higher-level, repeatable workflow for local pools and filesystems, particularly for developer or ephemeral workloads where speed and simplicity matter more than manual fine tuning.
Key Takeaway

Stratis abstracts complexity and accelerates local storage provisioning while still mapping to LVM and XFS under the hood. Inspect both layers when troubleshooting.

screens.title: iSCSI vs NFS — Client Troubleshooting Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: iSCSI and NFS are common protocols for sharing storage, but they differ in behavior and troubleshooting patterns. iSCSI exposes remote block devices so the client treats them like local disks. Troubleshoot client-side iSCSI issues by confirming iscsid is running, discovering targets with iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p target_IP, and logging in with iscsiadm -m node -l. Frequent problems are network reachability, firewall blocks, incorrect target credentials, or incorrect IQN configuration. NFS is a file protocol; clients mount exported paths. For NFS, confirm nfs-client. target is active on the client and use showmount -e server_IP to list exports. Mount option decisions (rw, sync, hard, intr) affect performance and failure modes. A common misconception is to treat iSCSI and NFS interchangeably; they have different semantics — iSCSI is block-level and sensitive to multipathing and SCSI reservations, while NFS is file-level and sensitive to client-server network latency and server locks. A concrete troubleshooting sequence for NFS: check network connectivity, validate server exports, verify mount options, and then consult server-side export and permission settings. For performance, measure latency, check server load, and ensure appropriate mount options. Always confirm both network and service state on client and server when diagnosing distributed storage issues.

narration.text: iSCSI and NFS are common protocols for sharing storage, but they differ in behavior and troubleshooting patterns. iSCSI exposes remote block devices so the client treats them like local disks. Troubleshoot client-side iSCSI issues by confirming iscsid is running, discovering targets with iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p target_IP, and logging in with iscsiadm -m node -l. Frequent problems are network reachability, firewall blocks, incorrect target credentials, or incorrect IQN configuration. NFS is a file protocol; clients mount exported paths. For NFS, confirm nfs-client. target is active on the client and use showmount -e server_IP to list exports. Mount option decisions (rw, sync, hard, intr) affect performance and failure modes. A common misconception is to treat iSCSI and NFS interchangeably; they have different semantics — iSCSI is block-level and sensitive to multipathing and SCSI reservations, while NFS is file-level and sensitive to client-server network latency and server locks. A concrete troubleshooting sequence for NFS: check network connectivity, validate server exports, verify mount options, and then consult server-side export and permission settings. For performance, measure latency, check server load, and ensure appropriate mount options. Always confirm both network and service state on client and server when diagnosing distributed storage issues.

keyIdea.title: Client Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Treat iSCSI as block-level with initiator/target operations and NFS as file-level with mount options; verify services, network, and permissions on both sides.

content.html:
Storage Network › Chapter 1.3 › iSCSI vs NFS
iSCSI — block protocol
Client sees remote storage as a block device. Initiator/target model requires discovery and login.
  • Key checks: iscsid service, iscsiadm discovery and login, firewall and routing.
  • Performance: watch multipathing and SCSI reservations for contention.
  • Example command: sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p <target_IP>
NFS — file protocol
Client mounts server exports. Mount options significantly influence behavior and performance.
  • Key checks: nfs-client.target, showmount -e server_IP, mount options such as rw, sync, hard.
  • Performance: network latency and server load often dominate.
  • Example command: sudo showmount -e <NFS_server_IP>
Common mistake
Treating NFS like a block device or expecting iSCSI to handle file-level locks the same way as NFS causes confusion. Use the right tool for the workload.
Key Takeaway
Verify services, network, and permissions on both client and server. Use protocol-specific tools for diagnostics.

screens.title: LUKS and cryptsetup — Encrypting Block Devices
screens.narratorSegment: LUKS provides a standardized container format for full-disk encryption on Linux. The cryptsetup utility provisions, opens, and manages LUKS containers. The essential workflow: run cryptsetup luksFormat on the block device to create a LUKS container, then cryptsetup luksOpen to map the encrypted device to /dev/mapper/yourname, create a filesystem there, and mount. A concrete example from the hands-on template uses sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb to encrypt and sudo cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb crypt_sdb to open. Key management is the critical operational consideration: losing the passphrase or keyslot data means complete data loss. For automated unlock at boot, add an entry to /etc/crypttab and consider integrating a TPM or network-based key escrow. A common misconception is that LUKS provides per-file encryption; it encrypts block devices, so file-level access controls still matter. Also remember to back up header information; cryptsetup allows backing up the LUKS header to enable recovery in some scenarios. Operational caution: test your cryptsetup and crypttab entries in a controlled environment before applying to production boot disks. Finally, verify cryptsetup status and device-mapper entries after configuration to confirm the mapping is correct.

keyIdea.text: Use cryptsetup to create and manage LUKS containers; protect and back up passphrases and headers as losing them means irreversible data loss.

content.html:
Security › Chapter 1.3 › LUKS / cryptsetup
LUKS workflow
Encrypt, open, format, mount, and integrate with crypttab for boot-time unlock.
# Encrypt device
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb

# Open it
sudo cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb crypt_sdb

# Create PV for LVM on the mapped device
sudo pvcreate /dev/mapper/crypt_sdb
Misconception
LUKS encrypts block devices, not individual files. You must still manage file permissions inside the filesystem.
Best practices
  • Back up LUKS headers and store passphrases securely off-host.
  • Test crypttab entries in a non-critical VM before deploying to boot disks.
  • Consider TPM or key escrow for automated unlock where appropriate.
Key Takeaway

LUKS secures data at rest when keys are managed properly. Losing keys or headers causes irreversible data loss.

screens.title: xfs_repair and fsck — Repair Tools and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystem repair tools differ by filesystem type and must be used with care. For XFS, the primary utility is xfs_repair, and it must only be run on an unmounted filesystem. Running xfs_repair on a mounted XFS can cause severe, irreversible corruption. For the ext family, fsck or e2fsck is used; fsck calls the correct tool for the filesystem type. A typical XFS repair: sudo xfs_repair /dev/mapper/myxfs_vol. For severe issues you may use sudo xfs_repair -L to zero the log, but that can discard recently committed metadata and lead to data loss; always attempt backups first. A concrete example: if an XFS filesystem becomes unmountable after a crash, boot a rescue environment, ensure the device is not mounted, and run xfs_repair. Misconceptions include thinking that filesystem repair tools are harmless; they can change on-disk state and must be used only when necessary and with backups. For ext filesystems, fsck can sometimes run in read-only or interactive modes; check man pages and prefer maintenance windows. The operational pattern: unmount, take a block-level backup if possible, run the filesystem-specific tool, review output, and then mount read-only initially to inspect data. This careful approach reduces the chance of compounding corruption.

keyIdea.text: Run xfs_repair only on unmounted XFS volumes; use fsck appropriately for ext filesystems and always back up before repairs when possible.

content.html:
Repair › Chapter 1.3 › xfs_repair & fsck
XFS repair rules
Use xfs_repair on unmounted XFS filesystems only. Consider -L only when necessary and after backups.
# Basic repair (unmounted)
sudo xfs_repair /dev/mapper/myxfs_vol

# Severe corruption (destructive)
sudo xfs_repair -L /dev/mapper/myxfs_vol
Precaution
If possible, take a block-level snapshot or backup before running destructive repair options.
fsck for non-XFS filesystems
fsck delegates to filesystem-specific checkers; prefer maintenance mode or unmounted state when possible.
  • Use fsck -n for a dry run when unsure.
  • During boot, fsck may run read-only checks; plan for downtime for repairs.
  • Always follow the filesystem-specific documentation for options and risks.
Warning

Never run xfs_repair on a mounted XFS filesystem. Doing so can make corruption worse or irrecoverable.

screens.title: Client Troubleshooting Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When a client reports storage connectivity or performance problems, use a repeatable triage to avoid missing simple causes. Step one: confirm basic network connectivity — ping the storage target and test routing and firewall rules. Step two: check service state on the client — for iSCSI ensure iscsid is active and for NFS ensure nfs-client. target is enabled. Step three: verify discovery and login — use iscsiadm for iSCSI discovery and showmount for NFS exports. Step four: inspect mount and device state with lsblk, mount, and df -h to see whether the device or export is mounted and how space is reported. Step five: measure latency and input and output around the problem using iostat, sar, or basic dd tests for throughput. A concrete example: an NFS-mounted directory appears slow; confirm network latency to the server, check server C P U and disk load, review server-side export options, and test alternate mount options such as switching from sync to async in a controlled test to see effects. Misconception: assuming only the network causes slowness; server load and export options frequently dominate. Follow the checklist methodically to isolate network, client, server, and filesystem factors.

keyIdea.text: Follow a consistent checklist: network, services, discovery, mounts, then performance measures to isolate iSCSI/NFS client issues quickly.

Troubleshooting › Chapter 1.3 › Client Checklist
Repeatable triage
Use this ordered checklist to isolate connectivity and performance causes quickly.
1 Network
Ping, traceroute, firewall rules, MTU mismatches.
2 Services
iscsid, nfs-client.target — ensure active.
3 Discovery
iscsiadm discovery or showmount -e for NFS.
4 Mounts
lsblk, mount, df -h to inspect state and usage.
5 Performance
iostat, dd, and sar to measure latency and throughput.
6 Logs
journalctl, server logs, and dmesg for kernel hints.
Key Takeaway

A methodical checklist prevents chasing symptoms and helps you escalate to server or network teams with concrete evidence.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: LUKS + LVM + Snapshot + VDO
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through a practical lab workflow that ties the chapter together. The lab assumes two raw devices: /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. First, install required packages like cryptsetup, lvm2, and vdo. Encrypt /dev/sdb with cryptsetup luksFormat and open it to create /dev/mapper/crypt_sdb. Initialize a physical volume on that mapper with pvcreate and create a volume group vg_appdata, then make a 5G logical volume lv_critical and format it with XFS. Mount to /mnt/appdata and create sample data. Create an LVM snapshot for lv_critical of size 1G, modify the data, then unmount and lvconvert --merge the snapshot to restore. For VDO, create a vdo instance on /dev/sdc with vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdc --vdoLogicalSize=10T, format the mapped device as XFS, mount it to /mnt/vdo_storage, and verify savings with vdostats. Important checks: confirm cryptsetup status and /dev/mapper entries, monitor lvs and pvs for snapshot usage, and use vdostats for real savings. Misconception: do not expect df -h to show VDO savings. The lab is destructive to the provided disks, so run it in an isolated VM. After the walkthrough, reflect on how snapshots enabled a fast rollback and how VDO provided logical size abstraction while saving physical space.

keyIdea.title: Lab Objective
keyIdea.text: Practice encrypting a disk, building LVM with a snapshot, and creating a VDO-backed filesystem, validating each step with status commands.

content.html:
Lab › Chapter 1.3 › Hands-on Script
Starter commands (annotated)
# 0. Install
sudo dnf install -y cryptsetup lvm2 vdo stratisd xfsprogs

# 1. LUKS on /dev/sdb
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb
sudo cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb crypt_sdb
sudo pvcreate /dev/mapper/crypt_sdb
sudo vgcreate vg_appdata /dev/mapper/crypt_sdb
sudo lvcreate --size 5G --name lv_critical vg_appdata
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/appdata
sudo mount /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical /mnt/appdata
Safety reminder
This script wipes devices. Run only in a disposable VM and back up any important data first.
Snapshot & VDO steps
# Create LV snapshot
sudo lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name lv_critical_snap /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical
# Modify data, then restore
sudo sh -c 'echo "Modified data" >> /mnt/appdata/data.txt'
sudo umount /mnt/appdata
sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical_snap
sudo mount /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical /mnt/appdata

# Create VDO on /dev/sdc
sudo vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdc --vdoLogicalSize=10T
sudo mkfs.xfs -K /dev/mapper/myvdo
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/vdo_storage
sudo mount /dev/mapper/myvdo /mnt/vdo_storage
sudo vdostats --human-readable
Verification
Confirm with lvs, pvs, vgs, cryptsetup status, df -h, and vdostats to ensure each step applied correctly.

screens.title: What to Remember — Storage Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the essentials helps retention. First: LVM snapshots are Copy-on-Write volumes that give point-in-time views. They are efficient but require sizing and monitoring because they only store changed blocks and can affect write performance. Second: VDO provides block-level deduplication and compression to reduce physical storage usage. Use vdostats, not df, to measure savings and monitor C P U and memory impact. Third: LUKS encrypts block devices using cryptsetup; losing passphrases or headers leads to irreversible data loss, so protect keys and test crypttab integrations. These three ideas — snapshot sizing and monitoring, VDO verification with vdostats, and careful LUKS key management — are the practical anchors you will apply in labs and production. When you face an incident, recall the safety checks: unmount before repairs, verify services for networked storage, and always back up critical metadata and keys before destructive operations.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter we focus on the storage tools and recovery skills you must master as an advanced RHEL administrator. You will learn how LVM snapshots give a point-in-time copy for safe backups and testing, how VDO provides deduplication and compression to lower storage costs, and how Stratis simplifies local pool and filesystem management. We also cover practical client-side troubleshooting for iSCSI and NFS, full-disk encryption with LUKS and cryptsetup, and the safe use of repair tools like xfs_repair and fsck. Each topic includes concrete commands and a hands-on scenario where you will encrypt a device, build an LVM with a snapshot, and create a VDO-backed filesystem. Why this matters: modern production systems rely on automated backups, efficient storage, and safe recovery procedures. Missteps such as running xfs_repair on a mounted filesystem or losing a LUKS passphrase can cause irreversible data loss. As you progress, practice the hands-on steps in a controlled VM environment and verify services and status commands. Keep the safety precautions in mind: confirm unmounted state before repairs, monitor snapshot sizes and input and output impact, and always back up encryption keys. Ready to explore the learning objectives and hands-on labs?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to create and manage LVM snapshots and weigh their performance implications in production. You will understand how VDO performs deduplication and compression and how to verify its effectiveness. You will also set up Stratis pools and filesystems to simplify local storage administration for ephemeral and developer workloads. For each objective you will practice commands and validation steps so the skill is actionable. For example, creating a snapshot requires choosing a size for the CoW area large enough to handle expected writes during the snapshot lifetime; we will walk through how to test this and monitor real input and output impact. You will also learn the practical reasons to prefer VDO for VM image stores and when to avoid it — such as when underlying device health is questionable. These objectives are focused on operational routines you will repeat in production, not just one-off demos.

This second objectives slide focuses on security and recovery: you will implement LUKS full-disk encryption and manage keys with cryptsetup, enabling automated unlock at boot when appropriate. You will practice creating encrypted PVs for LVM and understand the consequences of losing passphrases or not storing recovery keys. Additionally, you will learn the correct usage of filesystem repair tools: xfs_repair for XFS and fsck for other filesystems, including the important safety rule to run these tools only on unmounted filesystems or in rescue mode. The course also teaches verification commands such as lvs, vgs, pvs, cryptsetup status, df -h, and vdostats to validate configuration and health. A key part of mastery is understanding common mistakes — for example, merging a snapshot is destructive to current data and xfs_repair on a mounted XFS can create corruption. Each objective includes a hands-on verification step so you practice checks before making irreversible changes.

A logical volume snapshot is a copy-on-write view of an original logical volume that preserves the state at the time of snapshot creation. The technical mechanism is straightforward: when a snapshot exists, writes to the original volume are redirected so the snapshot keeps the pre-change blocks; the snapshot volume holds the original data until the copy-on-write happens. This allows you to take consistent backups without taking the application offline. A concrete example: create a snapshot with lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name myvol_snap /dev/vg_data/myvol. That snapshot will need enough space to store all changed blocks while it exists. A common misconception is to assume snapshots are full clones; they are not. They only consume additional space for blocks that change. Performance implications matter: the CoW mechanism adds input and output overhead on write paths, so snapshots on busy databases can cause latency. Key operational checks: monitor the snapshot usage with lvs or lvdisplay and plan snapshot lifetimes; ensure snapshot size covers expected write volume; and know that merging a snapshot is destructive to the current LV state, reverting it to the snapshot point in time. In short, snapshots are lightweight and powerful for backups and testing, but they require sizing, monitoring, and an understanding of their performance trade-offs. When would you choose a snapshot vs a full copy? Snapshots for short-lived backups and quick rollbacks; full copies for longer-term archival.

Here's a practical process you will use often: create a snapshot, modify the original data, and merge the snapshot to restore. First, ensure the logical volume is healthy and mounted where required. Create the snapshot with a size that accommodates expected writes: sudo lvcreate --size 1G --snapshot --name lv_critical_snap /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical. Confirm the snapshot with lvs and ensure the snapshot shows used and available space. Next, while the snapshot exists, you may modify files on the original LV to simulate a failed operation. After changes, if you need to revert, unmount the original filesystem: sudo umount /mnt/appdata. Then, merge the snapshot to revert the LV: sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_appdata/lv_critical_snap. This operation will apply the snapshot image back to the origin — it is destructive to newer changes. After merge completes, remount and verify. A concrete example: if a database write corrupts a table immediately after the snapshot, merging returns the data to the safe pre-change state. Misconception check: do not assume lvconvert --merge preserves new changes. It does not. Always have backups of critical data where possible and test snapshot merges in a controlled environment before using them in production.

VDO, the Virtual Data Optimizer, offers block-level deduplication and compression to reduce the physical storage required for logically large datasets. Think of it as a layer that presents a large logical device while storing fewer physical blocks by eliminating duplicate data and compressing unique blocks. A practical use case is a VM image store where many images share identical blocks; VDO can dramatically reduce physical usage. To create a VDO volume you run commands like sudo vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdb --vdoLogicalSize=10T and then make a filesystem on the mapped device. A common misconception is that df -h will show VDO savings; df reports the filesystem and device sizes the kernel exposes and won't show dedupe savings. Instead, use vdostats or vdostats --human-readable to measure 'Data Saved' and 'Savings %'. Troubleshooting VDO focuses on device health, ensuring the vdo service is running, and checking vdostats for abnormal activity. Also plan for C P U/memory overhead — deduplication and compression consume resources, so monitor system utilization. In short, VDO is powerful for repeatable block patterns, but validate savings with vdostats and confirm the underlying device is suitable for production workloads.

Managing VDO requires the right sequence: create the VDO device, format it, mount it, and monitor its statistics. After creating a VDO with vdo create, you typically run mkfs on the mapped device, for example sudo mkfs. xfs -K /dev/mapper/myvdo, and mount it to a path. Verification commands include vdostats to track logical and physical usage and vdo status or systemctl status vdo for service health. Troubleshooting often begins by confirming the vdo service is running and the underlying block device is healthy. If vdostats shows no savings, verify the data pattern is deduplicable and check for filesystem options that defeat compression. Another common issue is that df -h will show the device's physical size or logical size as presented; rely on vdostats to measure savings. For performance problems, check C P U and memory consumption since dedupe/compression require cycles. If the VDO device fails to start, inspect kernel messages and syslog for errors related to the device mapper. A concrete diagnostic command sequence is sudo vdo status; sudo vdostats --human-readable; sudo dmesg | tail to find kernel hints. Misconception: stopping a VDO device without unmounting can corrupt the filesystem mapped to /dev/mapper; always unmount before stopping VDO.

Stratis provides a higher-level interface for local storage management by creating pools of block devices and exposing filesystems within those pools. Under the covers it leverages existing primitives like LVM and XFS, but the administrator interacts with a simpler stratis CLI and a user-space daemon, stratisd. To create a pool you run sudo stratis pool create mypool /dev/sdd and then create a filesystem with sudo stratis filesystem create mypool myfs. Stratis aims to reduce administrative complexity for developer workflows, thin provisioning, and snapshots without needing manual LVM manipulation. A concrete example: when developers need ephemeral workspaces, Stratis pools let you provision filesystems quickly. Troubleshooting Stratis focuses on the stratisd service, stratis pool list, and stratis filesystem list to confirm configuration. A common misconception is that Stratis replaces all low-level tools — it orchestrates them and stores metadata in a managed layer. Because of that, understanding how Stratis maps to LVM and XFS is valuable when debugging underlying device issues. If a Stratis filesystem fails to mount, check stratisd logs and ensure the underlying block devices are present and healthy. How would you decide between Stratis and manual LVM? Use Stratis for quick, repeatable local pool management; use LVM directly when you need fine-grained control.

iSCSI and NFS are common protocols for sharing storage, but they differ in behavior and troubleshooting patterns. iSCSI exposes remote block devices so the client treats them like local disks. Troubleshoot client-side iSCSI issues by confirming iscsid is running, discovering targets with iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p target_IP, and logging in with iscsiadm -m node -l. Frequent problems are network reachability, firewall blocks, incorrect target credentials, or incorrect IQN configuration. NFS is a file protocol; clients mount exported paths. For NFS, confirm nfs-client. target is active on the client and use showmount -e server_IP to list exports. Mount option decisions (rw, sync, hard, intr) affect performance and failure modes. A common misconception is to treat iSCSI and NFS interchangeably; they have different semantics — iSCSI is block-level and sensitive to multipathing and SCSI reservations, while NFS is file-level and sensitive to client-server network latency and server locks. A concrete troubleshooting sequence for NFS: check network connectivity, validate server exports, verify mount options, and then consult server-side export and permission settings. For performance, measure latency, check server load, and ensure appropriate mount options. Always confirm both network and service state on client and server when diagnosing distributed storage issues.

LUKS provides a standardized container format for full-disk encryption on Linux. The cryptsetup utility provisions, opens, and manages LUKS containers. The essential workflow: run cryptsetup luksFormat on the block device to create a LUKS container, then cryptsetup luksOpen to map the encrypted device to /dev/mapper/yourname, create a filesystem there, and mount. A concrete example from the hands-on template uses sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb to encrypt and sudo cryptsetup luksOpen /dev/sdb crypt_sdb to open. Key management is the critical operational consideration: losing the passphrase or keyslot data means complete data loss. For automated unlock at boot, add an entry to /etc/crypttab and consider integrating a TPM or network-based key escrow. A common misconception is that LUKS provides per-file encryption; it encrypts block devices, so file-level access controls still matter. Also remember to back up header information; cryptsetup allows backing up the LUKS header to enable recovery in some scenarios. Operational caution: test your cryptsetup and crypttab entries in a controlled environment before applying to production boot disks. Finally, verify cryptsetup status and device-mapper entries after configuration to confirm the mapping is correct.

Filesystem repair tools differ by filesystem type and must be used with care. For XFS, the primary utility is xfs_repair, and it must only be run on an unmounted filesystem. Running xfs_repair on a mounted XFS can cause severe, irreversible corruption. For the ext family, fsck or e2fsck is used; fsck calls the correct tool for the filesystem type. A typical XFS repair: sudo xfs_repair /dev/mapper/myxfs_vol. For severe issues you may use sudo xfs_repair -L to zero the log, but that can discard recently committed metadata and lead to data loss; always attempt backups first. A concrete example: if an XFS filesystem becomes unmountable after a crash, boot a rescue environment, ensure the device is not mounted, and run xfs_repair. Misconceptions include thinking that filesystem repair tools are harmless; they can change on-disk state and must be used only when necessary and with backups. For ext filesystems, fsck can sometimes run in read-only or interactive modes; check man pages and prefer maintenance windows. The operational pattern: unmount, take a block-level backup if possible, run the filesystem-specific tool, review output, and then mount read-only initially to inspect data. This careful approach reduces the chance of compounding corruption.

When a client reports storage connectivity or performance problems, use a repeatable triage to avoid missing simple causes. Step one: confirm basic network connectivity — ping the storage target and test routing and firewall rules. Step two: check service state on the client — for iSCSI ensure iscsid is active and for NFS ensure nfs-client. target is enabled. Step three: verify discovery and login — use iscsiadm for iSCSI discovery and showmount for NFS exports. Step four: inspect mount and device state with lsblk, mount, and df -h to see whether the device or export is mounted and how space is reported. Step five: measure latency and input and output around the problem using iostat, sar, or basic dd tests for throughput. A concrete example: an NFS-mounted directory appears slow; confirm network latency to the server, check server C P U and disk load, review server-side export options, and test alternate mount options such as switching from sync to async in a controlled test to see effects. Misconception: assuming only the network causes slowness; server load and export options frequently dominate. Follow the checklist methodically to isolate network, client, server, and filesystem factors.

Now we walk through a practical lab workflow that ties the chapter together. The lab assumes two raw devices: /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. First, install required packages like cryptsetup, lvm2, and vdo. Encrypt /dev/sdb with cryptsetup luksFormat and open it to create /dev/mapper/crypt_sdb. Initialize a physical volume on that mapper with pvcreate and create a volume group vg_appdata, then make a 5G logical volume lv_critical and format it with XFS. Mount to /mnt/appdata and create sample data. Create an LVM snapshot for lv_critical of size 1G, modify the data, then unmount and lvconvert --merge the snapshot to restore. For VDO, create a vdo instance on /dev/sdc with vdo create --name=myvdo --device=/dev/sdc --vdoLogicalSize=10T, format the mapped device as XFS, mount it to /mnt/vdo_storage, and verify savings with vdostats. Important checks: confirm cryptsetup status and /dev/mapper entries, monitor lvs and pvs for snapshot usage, and use vdostats for real savings. Misconception: do not expect df -h to show VDO savings. The lab is destructive to the provided disks, so run it in an isolated VM. After the walkthrough, reflect on how snapshots enabled a fast rollback and how VDO provided logical size abstraction while saving physical space.

Summarizing the essentials helps retention. First: LVM snapshots are Copy-on-Write volumes that give point-in-time views. They are efficient but require sizing and monitoring because they only store changed blocks and can affect write performance. Second: VDO provides block-level deduplication and compression to reduce physical storage usage. Use vdostats, not df, to measure savings and monitor C P U and memory impact. Third: LUKS encrypts block devices using cryptsetup; losing passphrases or headers leads to irreversible data loss, so protect keys and test crypttab integrations. These three ideas — snapshot sizing and monitoring, VDO verification with vdostats, and careful LUKS key management — are the practical anchors you will apply in labs and production. When you face an incident, recall the safety checks: unmount before repairs, verify services for networked storage, and always back up critical metadata and keys before destructive operations.

Before you finish, keep three actionable reminders in mind. First: always unmount before running xfs_repair — running it on a mounted XFS can make corruption worse. Second: verify VDO savings using vdostats rather than relying on df; df cannot report deduplication or compression. Third: when using LUKS, back up passphrases and consider header backups so you can recover if a key is lost. These are not theoretical points — they are operational rules that prevent data loss and reduce incidents. In practice, combine these reminders with regular status checks such as lvs, vgs, pvs, cryptsetup status, and vdostats to maintain a healthy storage estate. Which of these will you add to your post-maintenance checklist? Key Concepts — Quick Reference means unmount before repair, measure vdo with vdostats, and back up luks keys and headers.. In practical terms, three actionable reminders before you finish. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
